Exploring a dataset with polyviz

polyviz-eda.Rmd

polyviz is built around a simple loop: look at the data, ask a question, draw the chart that answers it, repeat. This vignette walks that loop once, end to end, on pv_fiscal — a real dataset that ships with the package.

The data: who pays for whom in Canton Lucerne

Like most Swiss cantons, Lucerne runs a fiscal equalization scheme: municipalities with a strong tax base pay in, municipalities with a weak one receive support. pv_fiscal holds the key figures for every Lucerne municipality since 2020, published by LUSTAT Statistik Luzern:

  • resource_per_capita — tax resource potential per resident, in CHF;
  • resource_index — the same figure indexed so the cantonal average is 100;
  • equalization_chf — the equalization amount the municipality receives (0 for net contributors).

First look, before any chart:

pv_summary(pv_fiscal)
#> <pv_summary> 638 rows x 6 cols | 100.0% complete cases
#> 
#>  variable            class     n_missing pct_missing n_distinct
#>  year                integer   0         0             8       
#>  municipality_id     integer   0         0            82       
#>  municipality        character 0         0            82       
#>  resource_per_capita numeric   0         0           636       
#>  resource_index      numeric   0         0           432       
#>  equalization_chf    numeric   0         0           419       
#>  sketch                       
#>  2020 to 2027 (median 2023)   
#>  1001 to 1151 (median 1082)   
#>  top: Adligenswil (8)         
#>  1344 to 11448 (median 2732)  
#>  36.7 to 294 (median 75.4)    
#>  0 to 28287111 (median 679412)

About 80 municipalities per year (municipalities occasionally merge, so the count moves), no missing values, and years running from 2020 to 2027 — the last two of which are published projections, not accounts. pv_profile() gives the numeric columns a closer read:

pv_profile(pv_fiscal[c("resource_per_capita", "resource_index",
                       "equalization_chf")], engine = "r")
#>              variable   n n_missing         mean           sd     min      q25
#> 1 resource_per_capita 638         0 3.121480e+03 1.354719e+03 1343.73 2406.347
#> 2      resource_index 638         0 8.672962e+01 3.747845e+01   36.70   67.200
#> 3    equalization_chf 638         0 1.498420e+06 2.781096e+06    0.00    0.000
#>       median         q75         max skewness  kurtosis  jb_stat jb_p
#> 1   2731.545    3503.088    11448.39 2.754426 10.354253  3656.75    0
#> 2     75.400      95.500      293.70 2.707381  9.940827  3406.38    0
#> 3 679411.500 1965748.250 28287111.00 5.683642 42.384768 51191.09    0

Two things stand out. The resource index spans roughly 37 to 292 — the strongest municipality has almost eight times the per-resident tax resources of the weakest. And equalization_chf has a 25th percentile of 0: a sizeable minority of municipalities receive nothing at all.

How unequal is the tax base? 

f25 <- subset(pv_fiscal, year == 2025)

pv_histogram(
  f25, x = "resource_index",
  title = "Most Lucerne municipalities sit well below the average",
  subtitle = "Resource index, 2025 (cantonal average = 100)",
  source = "Quelle: LUSTAT Statistik Luzern"
) |>
  pv_annotate(pv_vline(100, label = "cantonal average"))

The distribution is heavily right-skewed. The bulk of municipalities cluster between roughly 50 and 90, below the average line; a long thin tail of lakeside communities — Meggen, Weggis, Vitznau — stretches past 200. Because the index weights by population, a handful of strong municipalities is enough to pull the average of 100 far above the median (about 74 in 2025).

Is that a snapshot quirk or a trend? Boxplots by year show the whole distribution moving:

pv_boxplot(
  pv_fiscal, value = "resource_index", group = "year",
  title = "The middle is drifting away from the top",
  subtitle = "Resource index by year; 2026-27 are projections",
  source = "Quelle: LUSTAT Statistik Luzern"
)

The median slides from about 78 in 2020 to about 70 in the 2027 projection, while the maximum barely moves. On this measure, dispersion is widening — which is exactly the situation equalization exists for.

Who receives, and how much? 

pv_scatter(
  f25, x = "resource_index", y = "equalization_chf",
  label = "municipality",
  title = "Payments fade out as the tax base approaches the average",
  subtitle = "Resource index vs. equalization received, 2025",
  ylab = "equalization (CHF)",
  source = "Quelle: LUSTAT Statistik Luzern"
) |>
  pv_trend("loess") |>
  pv_annotate(
    pv_vline(100, label = "cantonal average"),
    pv_note(65.9, 23278722, "Emmen", dx = -18, dy = 10)
  )

The broad shape is what the scheme promises: payments are concentrated below the average and reach zero near it. In 2025, 26 of 79 municipalities receive nothing, and none of them has an index under about 87.

But the scatter is honest about what the index alone does not explain. The largest single payment — about CHF 23 million to Emmen — goes to a municipality that is far from the poorest; Emmen is simply large, and equalization_chf is a total, not a per-resident amount. Among receivers, the correlation between index and amount is close to zero (-0.1), because population size dominates. A ranking of absolute amounts is therefore mostly a ranking of size:

top20 <- head(f25[order(-f25$equalization_chf), ], 20)

pv_lollipop(
  top20, x = "municipality", y = "equalization_chf",
  title = "The biggest cheques go to the biggest municipalities",
  subtitle = "Largest equalization payments, 2025 (CHF)",
  source = "Quelle: LUSTAT Statistik Luzern"
)

Where the weak tax bases are

The municipality numbers in pv_fiscal are official BFS ids, and the bundled pv_lucerne_map boundaries carry the same ids — so the join to a map is automatic:

pv_choropleth(
  f25, id = "municipality_id", value = "resource_index",
  title = "Tax resources follow the lake",
  subtitle = "Resource index by municipality, 2025 (average = 100)",
  source = "Quelle: LUSTAT Statistik Luzern; Grenzen: BFS ThemaKart"
)

The geography is stark: the strong tax bases hug Lake Lucerne and the agglomeration, while the rural north-west — the Napf hinterland around Romoos and Luthern — holds the weakest. Fiscal equalization in Lucerne is, to a first approximation, a transfer from the lakeshore to the hills.

Where to go next

  • The whole pipeline — CSV, SQLite, SAS, and the Python profiler — is covered in vignette("polyglot-backend").
  • pv_report() writes a one-call HTML report (summary, histograms, correlations) of any data frame, built from the same widgets used here.
  • Every chart above is interactive in the browser: hover for exact values, and in Shiny each chart also reports clicks (see ?pvchartOutput).
